say: An algorithm's defaults are a guess made by its authors about datasets in general, not about yours. Hyperparameter tuning searches for better ones. Optuna does that search with a Bayesian method rather than trying every combination.
The customer churn file again: two hundred and forty rows, nine features, predicting churned.
Tuning is per algorithm, not a competition, so you pick one. I am taking XGBoost, which has nine parameters worth searching.
Thirty trials by default. Each trial is one complete set of parameter values, cross validated. More trials find more, with diminishing returns and linearly more compute.

And the sampler is the part that makes this cleverer than a grid. Tree structured Parzen estimation builds a model of which regions of the parameter space produced good scores, and spends later trials there instead of sweeping uniformly.
There is the trial history, one point per trial, with the best one marked. The search improved the cross validation score over the untuned default.

And the parameter importance is the most useful thing on this screen. Optuna reports how much each parameter actually mattered to the outcome, and the answer is usually lopsided — one or two do nearly all the work while the rest barely move the score. That tells you what to search harder next time and what to leave alone.

And the number to be careful with is the cross validation score, because that is exactly what the search was optimising — it is an optimistic estimate by construction. These held-out metrics were measured after the search finished and took no part in it. They are the ones to quote.
And the tuned parameters download as JSON, so the run is reproducible rather than a number you have to trust.
